title: Rubbers explained: inverted, pimples and anti-spin
seo_title: Table tennis rubbers explained: inverted, pimples, anti
description: The types of table tennis rubber explained: inverted, short and long pimples and anti-spin, how each treats spin, what the rules allow and which to choose.
summary: Almost everyone plays with smooth inverted rubber, but pimpled and anti-spin rubbers change the ball in ways worth understanding. Here is how each works and what is legal.
key_points: Inverted rubber, smooth with the pimples facing in, grips the ball best and is what most players use on both sides.
Pimples-out rubber has a small contact area and is less affected by your opponent's spin.
Long pimples bend on contact and return the ball with unexpected spin; anti-spin has a low-friction smooth surface.
For competition a rubber must be on the ITTF's authorised list, matt, and black on one side with a bright colour on the other.
Nothing may be added to a rubber after it is made: speed glue and boosters are banned.
body: The rubber is the covering glued to each side of the blade, and it does more than anything else to decide how much spin you can make and how your opponent's spin affects you. There are four main types. Inverted rubber is smooth, with its pimples facing inwards, and grips the ball best; most players use it. Pimples-out (often called short pimples or short pips) and long pimples have their pimples facing out and handle spin differently. Anti-spin is smooth but slippery. As a beginner, use inverted rubber on both sides.
## How a rubber is made

The ITTF Laws allow two constructions. Ordinary pimpled rubber is a single sheet of solid rubber with pimples facing outwards, and no sponge. Sandwich rubber, the usual kind, is a layer of sponge with a sheet of pimpled rubber on top; the pimples can face in or out. Either way the pimples must be spread evenly at between 10 and 30 per square centimetre.

The Laws for 2026 also cap the thickness. Ordinary pimpled rubber must be less than 2.05mm thick including the glue, and sandwich rubber less than 4.05mm, with the top sheet no more than 2mm. Only one layer of sponge is allowed. Our guide to [sponge thickness and hardness](/guide/rubber-sponge-thickness-hardness.html) explains what the different sponges do.
## Inverted rubber

Inverted rubber is a sandwich rubber with the pimples turned inwards, towards the sponge, so the surface you hit with is smooth. Butterfly describes it as having "a large contact area for the ball, which makes it easy to impart spin". It is the standard for loops (heavy topspin strokes), serves with spin and almost every other shot in the modern game.

Within inverted rubbers there are two broad families. High-tension rubbers, such as Butterfly's Tenergy 05 and Rozena, are made with tension built into the rubber for extra elasticity, so the ball leaves them quickly. High-friction or tacky rubbers have a sticky surface that grips the ball; Butterfly's Dignics 09C, for example, combines high tension with what it calls "ball-holding tackiness". Our guide to [tacky and tensor rubbers](/guide/tacky-vs-tensor-rubbers.html) compares the two.
## Pimples-out

Turn the top sheet the other way and the pimples face the ball. Butterfly says pimples-out rubber has "a small contact area on the ball, which means it is less affected by the opponent's spin". You make less spin with it, but heavy spin from the other side comes back less strongly. Some pimples-out rubbers are sold without sponge, which Butterfly notes makes them light and low in bounce.
## Long pimples

Long pimples are tall in relation to their width, and they bend when the ball hits them. Butterfly says this produces an "unexpected variety of rotations", which makes the spin on the returned ball hard to read. Butterfly recommends its Feint Long III both for choppers, the defensive players who return the ball from far back with backspin, and for attacking players who stay close to the table.

The ITTF's technical rules for coverings classify a pimples-out rubber as long when its pimples' height divided by their diameter is more than 0.89, and no pimple may be more than 1.1 times as tall as it is wide. Long-pimpled rubbers come with thin sponge or none at all. Butterfly's Feint Long III, for example, is made with 1.3mm, 1.1mm or 0.5mm sponge, or in an "OX" version with no sponge.
## Anti-spin

Anti-spin rubber looks like inverted rubber, smooth with the pimples turned inwards, but its surface has very little grip. Butterfly describes it as "a rubber with less friction; it is less affected by the amount of spin applied by the opponent". It is a defensive rubber, usually on soft sponge, and a specialist choice.
## What the rules say

For league and tournament play, every rubber must be a brand and type currently authorised by the ITTF and fixed so that the ITTF logo and the maker's name are visible nearest the handle. The ITTF publishes the list of authorised racket coverings (LARC) twice a year, normally from 1 April and 1 October. Each entry is classed as in, out, long or anti.

The surface must be matt, with one side black and the other a bright colour clearly different from black and from the ball. Red is the traditional choice, and the list also includes rubbers in green, blue, pink and violet. The two colours let your opponent see which rubber you are using. Before a match, and whenever you change racket, you must let your opponent and the umpire examine it.

A rubber must also be used as it was authorised, with no physical or chemical treatment. Speed glues, solvent-based glues that players applied to their rubbers to add speed and spin, were banned from 1 September 2008 because of health concerns, and the ITTF announced at the same time that boosters and tuners, rubs that do a similar job, were banned too. Players must glue their rubbers on with glue that contains no harmful volatile solvents, and at events with racket control, rackets are tested before matches. Our guide to [approved rubbers and the racket rules](/guide/ittf-approved-rubbers-and-racket-rules.html) covers the detail.
## Which should you choose?

Play with inverted rubber on both sides for at least your first year. It lets you learn every stroke, including spin serves and loops, and makes it easier to read what other rubbers are doing when you meet them. Choose a softer, thinner version to start; Butterfly's own guidance rates soft sponge as suited to beginners. Pimples and anti-spin are worth trying later, ideally with advice from a coach at your [club](/guide/find-a-table-tennis-club-england.html).

If you are still choosing your first bat, start with [what bat to buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html); if you want to understand the blade underneath, read [blades explained](/guide/table-tennis-blades-explained.html).
